opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so my first reaction was honestly skepticism. When someone tells you a model has produced something that looks like a genuinely new result, the prior has to be that something went wrong somewhere. Maybe the problem statement was subtly different from what we thought, maybe there's a gap in the argument that's easy to miss, or maybe it's actually a known result that just isn't well-known to us. So the first thing was to not get excited and instead try to break it.

What made Lijie and Hongxun so valuable here is that they're real experts in the area. They weren't just reading the output and saying "this looks plausible." They were going through it line by line, checking each step the way you would if you were refereeing a paper. With these models, the writing can be very fluent and confident, and that's exactly when you have to be most careful, because a confident-sounding proof can still hide a step that doesn't actually follow.

So the process was really: first, pin down exactly what's being claimed and make sure it's the statement we care about. Second, have people who know the field verify the argument independently, ideally more than one person. Third, look at the literature and ask colleagues whether this is already known, because "new to us" isn't the same as "new." And only after it survived all of that did we start to believe it.

I think that's the right posture in general as these systems get more capable. The bar for "this is real" should stay high. But it was also a pretty remarkable moment when it held up, because it was a sign that these models are starting to contribute things that experts find genuinely interesting, not just reproduce what's already out there.

r001.rationale: He says his first reaction was skepticism and that an apparent new result should prompt checking for a mistake, such as a gap or misstatement.

r002.rationale: The response says belief came only after the result survived verification, but does not say his optimism increased as days passed without finding a bug.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was skepticism, because that's the reflex you build up doing research. When something looks that clean, you assume there's a bug somewhere, either in the problem setup or in how the result got checked. So the first thing I did was ask them to send me the exact prompt and the full output, not a summary of it. I wanted to see what the model had actually been given and what it had actually written, word for word.

Then I tried to break it. I read the argument the way I'd read a referee submission, looking for the step where it hand-waves or quietly assumes the thing it's trying to prove. With these problems there's almost always a lemma that looks innocent and is doing all the work, so I went straight for those and tried to construct counterexamples. I also wanted to rule out contamination. If this were a known result sitting in some paper or lecture notes, the model reproducing it would be much less interesting, so we spent a while checking whether anything close to it had been published.

And then the boring but important part: reproduce it. Rerun it independently, vary the phrasing, see whether the model finds the same argument or just stumbled into it once. A single lucky sample tells you very little. Consistency across runs tells you a lot more.

What convinced me in the end wasn't the final answer, it was the structure of the reasoning. The proof held up to the kind of poking that usually makes these things fall apart, and Lijie and Hongxun had already done a lot of that themselves before bringing it to me. That's really the bar. Not "does it look impressive," but "can a careful expert who wants it to be wrong fail to make it wrong."

r001.rationale: He says his first reaction was skepticism and that a result this clean made him assume there was a bug.

r002.rationale: He describes checking and reproducing the result, but does not say his confidence grew over days without finding a bug.

astra-6.text: My first reaction was skepticism—not because I doubted them, but because the result sounded so strong that I wanted to understand exactly what was being claimed. The key was to look past the headline and work through the argument: what were the assumptions, where was the crucial new idea, and did that step actually give the conclusion? A surprising result isn’t necessarily wrong, but you want your confidence to come from the proof rather than from how plausible the statement sounds.
